# Aristotelian Temporality and Motion: Philosophical Foundations for Rhetorical Being

## 1. Articulate Aristotle's Understanding of Motion and Time

Aristotle's conception of motion emerges not as a simple mechanical displacement, but as a fundamental ontological structure that determines the very character of being-in-the-world; indeed, his understanding of kinesis reveals itself to be intimately connected to the temporal constitution of existence itself. 115), thus establishing motion as the fundamental temporal structure through which beings encounter their world. This  Aristotle's understanding transcends the modern mechanistic view of motion as mere spatial displacement; rather, motion constitutes the very condition under which beings can be present to themselves and to others within their temporal horizons. The significance of this understanding becomes apparent when we recognize that for Aristotle, the study of nature itself depends upon grasping motion correctly, for as Heidegger observes in his analysis of Aristotelian philosophy, the researcher "gradually became compelled by truth itself to see beings" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 176). Thus, motion emerges as the pathway through which beings disclose themselves in their temporal unfolding, making possible the very encounter with truth that characterizes authentic philosophical inquiry. ## 2. 27),  essential ambiguity between activity and passivity that characterizes all genuine motion. This definition deliberately confounds expectations about Aristotelian categorization by suggesting that the thing moved possesses its own capacity for movement while simultaneously being moved by another; hence, the moved thing is not merely passive but participates actively in its own transformation. The temporal implications of this understanding become evident when we consider that motion, as Heidegger emphasizes, "should be understood as a fundamental way that Dasein is" rather than as something external to being itself (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 27). Consequently, motion emerges not as an accidental property of beings but as the very mode through which beings exist temporally, encountering themselves and their world through the dynamic interplay of capacity and actualization that characterizes their finite, temporal existence. ## 3. Aristotle on Time

Aristotle's understanding of time emerges from his analysis of motion, yet it reveals distinctive characteristics that illuminate the temporal structure of consciousness itself; specifically, time manifests as the measure through which change becomes intelligible to beings who exist within temporal horizons. Heidegger's  the Greek understanding of being fundamentally involves "being-present (Anwesenheit)" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 262), indicating that temporality functions not merely as a framework within which beings appear, but as the very condition of their appearing as such. 115). The temporal structure of fear reveals itself as fundamentally oriented toward the future, yet this futural orientation requires the present synthesis of imagination to make the not-yet-present threat somehow present to consciousness. Thus, Aristotle's conception of time involves the complex interplay between presence and absence, actuality and potentiality, that characterizes temporal consciousness in its encounter with both past experiences and future possibilities. ## 4. The Relation Between Motion and Time

The fundamental relationship between motion and time in Aristotelian philosophy reveals itself through the recognition that temporal experience emerges only through the encounter with change, while motion itself becomes intelligible only within temporal horizons; accordingly, neither motion nor time can be adequately understood in isolation from the other. Burke's analysis illuminates this relationship by suggesting that transformation itself requires temporal structure, for (Hawhee 2011) in his discussion of dramatic imagery, the essence of things reveals itself through their temporal unfolding toward completion or fulfillment (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, p. 27). This  the relationship between motion and time involves more than mere correlation; rather, they constitute co-originary aspects of the same fundamental phenomenon—the temporal becoming through which beings encounter their own possibilities. Rickert's ambient rhetoric provides additional insight into this relationship by emphasizing that kairos itself "needs to be thought of ambiently, akin to Heidegger's understanding of the Umwelt, or the surrounding world" (Rickert, *Ambient Rhetoric*, p. 108), thus indicating that temporal experience always occurs within situated environments that themselves possess temporal rhythms and durations. The significance of this co-originary relationship becomes apparent when we recognize that rhetorical effectiveness depends not merely upon appropriate timing but upon attunement to the temporal rhythms through which audiences experience their own situated existence; hence, the relationship between motion and time provides the ontological foundation for understanding how discourse can achieve genuine persuasive power through temporal attunement rather than mere manipulation. ## 5. Aisthēsis and Temporal Awareness

Aristotelian aisthesis reveals its essentially temporal character through the recognition that perception always involves the synthesis of temporal moments, making possible the awareness of change and continuity that characterizes conscious experience; thus, sensory awareness emerges not as passive reception but as active temporal constitution. Burke's analysis of symbolic transformation provides insight into this temporal dimension by emphasizing that perception involves ongoing processes of identification and differentiation that unfold through time (Burke, *A Grammar of Motives*, p. 302). This temporal synthesis becomes particularly evident in Heidegger's analysis of the passions, where (Hawhee 2011) emotional awareness involves complex temporal orientations—fear, for instance, involves present awareness of future possibilities that may or may not actualize (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115). The significance of this temporal structure lies in its revelation that consciousness itself possesses an essentially rhetorical character, insofar as it involves ongoing processes of interpretation and response that unfold through encounters with otherness. Furthermore, aisthesis reveals itself as fundamentally attuned to the temporal rhythms of the world itself; accordingly, genuine perception involves not merely the reception of sensory data but attunement to the temporal patterns through which the world discloses itself to consciousness. This  temporal awareness possesses an essentially ecological character, involving responsive engagement with environmental temporalities rather than subjective imposition of temporal categories upon an essentially atemporal world. ## 6. Phantasia and Temporal Unification

Phantasia emerges in Aristotelian psychology as the faculty through which temporal synthesis becomes possible, enabling consciousness to unify past experiences, present perceptions, and future anticipations into coherent temporal wholes; indeed, phantasia functions as the temporal bridge that makes possible both memory and anticipation. 5), thus suggesting that imaginative synthesis involves more than mere combination of discrete temporal moments. Rather, phantasia enables the recognition of temporal patterns and rhythms that provide the foundation for both practical judgment and rhetorical effectiveness; hence, the temporal unification achieved through phantasia makes possible the kind of situated reasoning that characterizes phronesis. Burke's rhetorical theory illuminates this temporal dimension by emphasizing that symbolic action always involves transformational processes that unfold through time (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, p. 28), suggesting that rhetorical discourse achieves its effects through engaging the temporal syntheses that phantasia makes possible. The significance of this understanding lies in its recognition that rhetorical persuasion operates not merely through logical argument but through engagement with the temporal imagination that enables audiences to envision alternative possibilities for their own existence. Multiple authors in the Heidegger and Rhetoric  this temporal unification involves not merely cognitive synthesis but affective attunement that enables beings to respond appropriately to their situated temporal existence (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 26). Thus, phantasia reveals itself as the temporal faculty through which beings achieve coherent engagement with their own finite, temporal existence while remaining open to the transformational possibilities that emerge through rhetorical encounter. ## 7. Heidegger's Interpretation of Aristotle

Heidegger's interpretation of Aristotelian philosophy reveals temporal existence as fundamentally characterized by care and concern, indicating that human being-in-the-world involves essentially temporal structures of projection and throwness that determine the possibilities for authentic existence; accordingly, his  Aristotelian insights anticipate fundamental existential-ontological structures. In *Being and Time*, Heidegger develops this interpretation by showing how temporal ecstases provide the horizon within which beings can encounter themselves and their world authentically (Heidegger, *Being and Time*, p. 262). His analysis in *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy* further illuminates this temporal structure by emphasizing that "living means being-in-a-world" where temporal awareness emerges through situated engagement rather than detached contemplation (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 177). This interpretation reveals that Aristotelian psychology already contains insights into the temporal structure of existence that modern philosophy has often obscured through its emphasis on consciousness as purely cognitive faculty; indeed, Heidegger's  the passions reveal temporal structures that are more fundamental than cognitive processes. The significance of this interpretation lies in its demonstration that Aristotelian philosophy provides resources for understanding human existence as essentially temporal and finite, thus avoiding both the abstractions of idealistic philosophy and the reductions of naturalistic psychology. Furthermore, Heidegger's interpretation reveals how the Aristotelian understanding of motion and time provides the ontological foundation for understanding rhetoric as more than mere technique—rather, as fundamental attunement to the temporal conditions under which human existence unfolds; hence, authentic rhetorical practice requires ontological understanding of the temporal structures that make possible genuine encounter between speakers and audiences within their shared temporal horizons. ---
